ARTICLE IN PRESS Decoding Apathy in the Middle-Aged and Older Adults: The Indirect Effect of Loneliness and the Moderating Effect of Cognitive Function on Resilience ABSTRACT Apathy, a multi-dimensional construct characterized by diminished motivation and emotional indifference, is a prevalent yet underexplored condition in middle-aged and older adults. This multi-faceted condition significantly impacts daily activities and overall well-being. While resilience and cognitive abilities have been proposed as potential protective factors against apathy, their interplay with the condition remains poorly understood. This study aimed to investigate the indirect effect of resilience on multi-dimensional apathy via loneliness and to assess further whether this indirect effect is moderated by cognitive function. A cohort of 218 community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older was recSruited. Participants provided demographic information and completed validated quesStionnaires to assess resilience, loneliness, and multi-dimensional apathy, along with perEformance-based cognitive tests. The R moderated mediation model was analyzed using the PROCESS macro in SPSS. Our findings P revealed that loneliness accounted for a statistically significant indirect effect in the association between resilience and multi-dimensional apNathy, specifically for the domains of Cognitive I and Social Motivation (B = -0.046, 95% CI [-0.08, -0.02]) and Spontaneous Behavioral Activation (B = -0.024, 95% CI [-0.0E4, -0.01]). Notably, cognitive function moderated the L indirect association between resilience and multi-dimensional apathy via loneliness (B = -0.070, C p < 0.001, 95% CI [-0.11, -0.03]), indicating that the indirect influence of resilience on multi- I faceted apathy diminishedT with declining cognitive function. By uncovering the intricate R relationships between resilience, loneliness, multi-dimensional apathy, and cognitive function, A our study offers groundbreaking insights into combating apathy in the aging population. The emphasis on enhancing resilience and cognitive capabilities presents a forward-thinking approach to mitigating the adverse effects of loneliness, heralding a new direction in fostering a resilient and cognitively engaged elderly community. Keywords: mental health, resilience, apathy, loneliness, cognitive function, middle-aged and older adults. 1 ARTICLE IN PRESS 1. Introduction The rapid aging of the global population represents a significant demographic shift (Partridge et al., 2018). Projections indicate that by 2050, individuals aged 65 and older will comprise nearly 16% of the worldwide population, nearly doubling the proportion of children under five (Gerland et al., 2022). This trend, driven by increased life expectancy and reduced mortality rates, underscores the importance of addressing aging-related medical conditions, such as neurodegenerative diseases (Yu et al., 2020; Yu & Wu, 2022) and mental health problems (World Health Organization, 2023), which can significantly impair daily functioning and reduce life quality in later years(Chen et al., 2022; Dogra et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2015). Therefore, a detailed understanding of mental health challenges among older adults is vital for enhancing the effectiveness of healthcare services. A significant focus of research in this area has been apathy, defined as a state of diminished S motivation, emotion, and interest (Marin, 1991, 1996). Evidence supports a multi-dimensional S view of apathy encompassing cognitive, behavioral, and emotional components (Levy & E Dubois, 2006; Marin et al., 1991; Robert et al., 20R09). Levy and Dubois (2006) describe cognitive apathy as difficulty in formulating actiPon plans for impending behaviors, while emotional apathy is characterized by a lack of pos itive or negative emotions due to an inability N to link emotional signals with forthcoming actions. Behavioral apathy, also referred to as ‘auto- I activation deficit’, is characterized by an i nability to initiate thoughts or actions independently. E Recent research has further proposed the concept of social apathy, defined as a reduction in L initiative to propose or engage inC social activities or interactions (Stuss et al., 2000), noting its I presence in nearly one-quarter of patients with mild neurocognitive disorders (Manera et al., T 2019). R Apathy may prAesent as a secondary manifestation associated with mood disorders, cognitive dysfunction, or diminished levels of consciousness (Marin, 1991), or may emerge as a distinct clinical feature in the context of neurodegenerative disorders (Miller et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2020), psychiatric disorders (Amodio et al., 2018; Bortolon et al., 2018), and even normative aging (Fazio et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2021). For older adults, even those without clinical conditions, apathy is linked with an increased risk of dementia (Bock et al., 2020), disability (Ayers et al., 2017), and mortality (Eurelings et al., 2018). Despite its significance, apathy is less frequently recognized in clinical settings compared to more disruptive symptoms (van der Linde et al., 2017), highlighting the importance of understanding its underlying causes and mechanisms. Although apathy may increase with age, it is not an inevitable outcome. Psychological resources such as resilience may help protect against its development by buffering the impact of psychosocial stressors. Resilience, defined as the capacity to adapt positively in the face of adversity (Luthar et al., 2000), serves as a protective factor by promoting motivation and active coping among older adults (Fredrickson, 2001; Madsen et al., 2019). It is positively associated 2 ARTICLE IN PRESS with self-efficacy, mental health, and social support, and negatively associated with loneliness, psychological distress, and perceived stress in community-dwelling older adults (Górska et al., 2022). Consistent with these findings, prior studies have demonstrated that individuals with higher resilience tend to report lower levels of loneliness (Balki et al., 2023; Gerino et al., 2017; Xie et al., 2022). However, apathy is not uniformly present among individuals with low resilience, suggesting that other intervening mechanisms—particularly loneliness—may shape the relationship between resilience and apathy. Loneliness is a well-documented psychosocial risk factor that negatively affects the well- being of older adults living in the community (Van As et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2018). From a social neuroscience perspective, loneliness may trigger an increase in depressive symptoms, functioning as a nonverbal signal that reflects the need for social connection and affiliation (Cacioppo et al., 2014). While apathy and depression share overlapping features, such as reduced interest and diminished activity, they are conceptually aSnd neurobiologically distinct. Depression is typically characterized by persistent negaStive affect—including sadness, hopelessness, and guilt—whereas a lack of motivation, iEnitiative, and emotional engagement R in the absence of negative mood defines apathy. Neuroimaging studies have further validated P this distinction, revealing that the two conditions involve dissociable neural circuits (Lanctôt et al., 2023). Significantly, loneliness may coNntribute to apathy through mechanisms that are I independent of depression. It has been shown to reduce social motivation (Vanhalst et al., 2018) and increase social withdrawal (PreeceE et al., 2021), both of which are key components of the L behavioral profile associated with apathy. C Thus, beyond its association with depressive symptoms, loneliness may exert a distinct I influence on the developmTent of apathy. Given that resilience is negatively associated with R loneliness (Jackson et al., 2023; Ribeiro-Gonçalves et al., 2023), and loneliness is positively A associated with apathy (Cristofori et al., 2019; McDaniels et al., 2023), it is reasonable to hypothesize that loneliness serves as an indirect pathway linking resilience to apathy. Cognitive function is another pivotal aspect, with higher cognitive function linked to various benefits, including a positive relationship with the physical domain of quality of life (Hsiao et al., 2016) and reduced mortality rates (Lv et al., 2019). According to the cognitive model of resilience proposed by Pearsons et al. (2016), optimally flexibly employing cognitive- affective systems facilitates resilient responses. Resilience thus requires high cognitive abilities and adaptability to properly modulate responses in a given situation. Therefore, an interaction effect may exist between cognitive function and resilience, leading to different coping outcomes and diverse emotional consequences. In summary, the interplay between resilience, loneliness, and cognitive function likely shapes the manifestation of apathy in older adults, but the precise mechanistic influences remain unclear. Drawing on both theoretical frameworks and empirical evidence, the present study proposes a structured model in which resilience serves as a protective psychological 3 ARTICLE IN PRESS resource, reducing the likelihood of experiencing loneliness—a situational state known to diminish motivation and social engagement. Prior research has shown that individuals with higher resilience report lower levels of loneliness, and that loneliness, in turn, is linked to motivational deficits characteristic of apathy. On this basis, loneliness was modeled as a mediator in the relationship between resilience and apathy. By contrast, cognitive function was conceptualized as a moderator, in line with the cognitive resilience framework, which posits that the ability to deploy cognitive and affective resources flexibly is essential for effective adaptation to stressors. Individuals with higher cognitive functioning may be better able to leverage resilience to regulate loneliness and reduce apathy, whereas cognitive impairment may attenuate this capacity. This conceptual model guided our use of a moderated mediation analysis to examine whether loneliness explains the indirect association between resilience and multi-dimensional apathy, and whether this indirect pathway is contingent upon an individual’s level of cognitive function. The study successfully enrolled 218 middle-aged and older adults residing in the community, all of whom provided written informed consent before participating. 2.2. Measurement 2.2.1. Sociodemographic Profiling and Assessment of Depressive Symptoms in Middle-Aged and Older Adults Population This research involved collecting data on age, gender, socioeconomic status, marital status, and living arrangements. SES was determined through a combination of educational and occupational factors, categorized into five levels. The SES index is computed by quadrupling the education score and adding it to seven times the occupation score, resulting in a range of 11 to 55 (Lin, 2005). Marital status was classified as married and unmarried (i.e., single, divorced, and widowed). Living conditions were assessed based on whether individuals cohabited with a spouse, children, or other relatives, or lived alone. Additionally, the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15) (Sheikh & Yesavage, 1986) was used as a control variable in our study to measure depressive symptoms, thereby ensuring the accurate assessment of 4 ARTICLE IN PRESS apathy symptoms. 2.2.2. Apathy To evaluate apathy, two instruments were employed: the Geriatric Apathy Scale (GAS) (Yi et al., 2024) and the Apathy Evaluation Scale, clinician version (AES-C) (Marin et al., 1991). The GAS, a newly developed instrument tailored for the Chinese elderly and considering cultural nuances, consists of 16 items covering three apathy subcomponents: Cognitive and Social Motivation (CSM), which refers to reduced interest in planning, goal setting, or initiating interactions (e.g. “I will choose to participate in leisure activities that I am interested in”), Emotional Response and Expression (ERE), reflecting diminished emotional reactivity or reduced display of affect (e.g., “I feel guilty if I find myself treating others badly“), and Spontaneous Behavioral Activation (SBA), indicating decreased self-initiated behavior, such as engaging in daily tasks without external prompting (e.g., “Before going out to participate in activities, I will prepare myself in advance”). EaSch item is rated on a 4-point Likert scale, with scores ranging from 0 to 48, where higher scSores indicate more severe apathy. Given the novelty of GAS, the AES was also utilizeEd as a benchmark for accurate apathy R measurement. The AES is a broadly used tool to assess general apathy levels, available in self- P rated (AES-S), clinician-rated (AES-C), and informant-rated (AES-I) versions. It comprises 18 items, each scored on a 4-point Likert scale, Nwith total scores ranging from 18 to 72, where I higher scores denote more severe apathy. 2.2.3. Resilience E L The Resilience Scale for Older Adults (RSOA) (Li & Ow, 2022) was implemented to C gauge resilience in community-dwelling older adults. The scale incorporates four dimensions: I personal strength, meaningT and purpose of life, family support, and social support. Each item R is rated using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = never, 2 = rarely, 3 = sometimes, 4 = usually, 5 = A always). The overall score ranges from 15 to 60, with higher scores indicating stronger resilience. 2.2.4. Loneliness Loneliness was measured using the Elderly Loneliness Scale (Lin & Lin, 2013). This 10- item scale assesses feelings of social and emotional loneliness, scored on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 1(“strongly disagree”) to 4 (“strongly agree”). The total score varies from 10 to 40, with higher scores representing greater feelings of loneliness. The internal consistency of the total scale was 0.86, while the subscales of social and emotional loneliness were 0.87 and 0.62, respectively. 2.2.5. Cognitive function Cognitive function in the participants was evaluated using the Chinese version of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) (Folstein et al., 1975; Yu et al., 2022), a 30-item screening tool that covers six domains: orientation, attention, memory, language, visual construction, and comprehension and praxis. The maximum score is 30, with higher scores 5 ARTICLE IN PRESS indicative of better cognitive functioning. 2.2.6. Statistical analysis Descriptive analyses were employed to characterize the sociodemographic attributes of the study population. The prevalence of apathy, as measured by the AES and GAS, was compared using an independent t-test and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Pearson correlation analyses were conducted to examine the relationships among key study variables, including resilience, loneliness, cognitive function, overall apathy, the three subcomponents of apathy as per GAS, and depressive symptoms. The moderation and moderated mediation models were analyzed using the PROCESS macro in SPSS (Hayes, 2013), employing 5,000 bootstrap resamples to establish a 95% bias-corrected confidence interval. The indirect effect of loneliness on the relationship between resilience and multi- dimensional apathy was initially examined using Model 4, with significance determined by the 95% confidence interval of the indirect effect, excluding zero. SuSbsequently, Model 7 was then applied to explore cognitive function as a moderator in the Sresilience-loneliness relationship. Additionally, the Johnson-Neyman technique (Carden et aEl., 2017; Hayes & Rockwood, 2017) R delineated conditional indirect effects and confidence bands. All statistical analyses were P executed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Macintosh, version 28.0. A two-tailed p-value of less than 0.05 was considered indicative of statisticNal significance. Discussion We examined the intricate relationship between resilience, loneliness, and cognitive function, as well as their combined impact on the multifaceted phenomenon of apathy among middle-aged and older adults. Our findings highlight the indirect role of loneliness in the 7 ARTICLE IN PRESS association between resilience and apathy, suggesting that individuals with higher resilience are less likely to experience apathy in part because they are more protected against loneliness. Notably, this indirect effect was explicitly observed in the apathy dimensions of Cognitive and Social Motivation and Spontaneous Behavioral Activation. Moreover, cognitive function moderated this indirect effect, with higher cognitive function intensifying the impact of resilience on reducing loneliness and apathy. Our findings highlight the critical role that psychological resilience and cognitive functioning play as intrinsic resources for middle-aged and older adults in managing the stress of loneliness without succumbing to apathy. Through mediation analysis, we identified a significant indirect association between resilience and apathy, mediated by loneliness, suggesting that resilience may influence apathy indirectly through its relationship with loneliness. This study pioneers the delineation of the interplay between resilience, loneliness, and apathy. We established that loneliness independently affects apathy, beyond its impacts on depressive sSymptoms. This aligns with the findings of Groeneweg-Koolhoven et al. (2014), which iSndicated that, in the absence of depressive symptoms and cognitive impairment, lonelineEss was more pronounced in middle- R aged and older adults with apathy compared to those without. This study, however, did not find P significant differences in loneliness among those without cognitive impairment but with depressive symptoms. N I Recent advancements in research have led to apathy being segmented into distinct dimensions, enhancing our understandiEng of its underlying mechanisms. Our study contributed L to this body of knowledge by examining whether loneliness serves as an indirect pathway C linking resilience to the multi-faceted components of apathy, explicitly focusing on Cognitive I and Social Motivation, EmTotional Response and Expression, and Spontaneous Behavioral R Activation. We discovered that accounted for the indirect associations between psychological A resilience and both Cognitive and Social Motivation apathy and Spontaneous Behavioral Activation apathy, with the direct effects becoming non-significant when loneliness was included in the model. However, this effect was not observed in Emotional Response and Expression apathy. The absence of an indirect effect in the Emotional Response and Expression domain may reflect distinct neural mechanisms underpinning this subtype of apathy. Unlike cognitive and behavioral apathy, which have been closely linked to dysfunction in the prefrontal cortex and dorsal basal ganglia circuits, emotional apathy appears to rely more on limbic and reward- related pathways, including the orbitofrontal cortex and ventral striatum. These regions are implicated in the processing of emotional salience and reward sensitivity, which may be relatively preserved in healthy aging. For example, Castel et al. (2016) found that older adults retained the ability to prioritize emotionally salient monetary cues in memory tasks, while Yee et al. (2019) demonstrated that older individuals continued to rely on specific incentive types— such as monetary rewards—to enhance cognitive performance, despite age-related changes in 8 ARTICLE IN PRESS motivational integration. Furthermore, evidence from clinical populations supports the notion that emotional apathy operates via mechanisms distinct from those driving other apathy subtypes. In a study of individuals with Parkinson’s disease, Ang et al. (2018) reported that emotional apathy was not significantly associated with depressive symptoms, in contrast to the stronger links observed for behavioral and social apathy. In contrast, Raffard et al. (2016) reported different findings in a non-demented older adult sample. Their path analysis revealed that cognitive apathy, compared to behavioral and emotional apathy, shared a greater number of contributing factors, including anticipatory pleasure, reward sensitivity, cognitive functioning, and physical functioning. Such findings underscore the importance of considering apathy as a multi-dimensional construct and suggest that emotional apathy may be less susceptible to psychosocial factors, such as loneliness, particularly when emotional reward systems remain intact. Taken together, these neurobehavioral distinctions may eSxplain why the hypothesized indirect pathway from resilience to apathy through lonelinesSs did not emerge in the emotional domain. Our findings thus support a differentiated underEstanding of apathy and highlight the R value of examining its component processes separately, especially when considering potential P intervention targets for older adults. Moreover, our moderated mediation Nanalysis of the indirect association between I resilience and apathy, mediated by loneliness, varied as a function of cognitive function. This effect was consistent across both the GEAS and the AES scales, suggesting that the GAS is just L as reliable as the AES in measuring these constructs. As predicted by the cognitive resilience C model, cognitive function buffered the positive influence of resilience on coping with stress I (e.g., loneliness), aligning Twith a previous study that demonstrated a correlation between R resilience and better cognition (McDaniel et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2021). Conversely, a A contrasting finding revealed that middle-aged and older adults may encounter the highest level of loneliness when they possess high cognitive function but low resilience. From a cognitive resilience model perspective, these situations may arise due to the incapacity to regulate responses to specific situations through cognitive processing (Parsons et al., 2016). While cognitive function has been positively associated with psychological resilience, our findings suggest that this relationship may not always yield protective benefits in the absence of adequate emotional coping resources. The observed loneliness among older adults with high cognitive function but low resilience may reflect a mismatch between the capacity for cognitive processing and the ability to engage those strategies for emotion regulation. This interpretation aligns with the cognitive resilience framework (Parsons et al., 2016), which posits that cognitive abilities provide a foundation for adaptive regulation, but their benefits may not be realized if individuals lack the psychosocial means to deploy them effectively. Additionally, we observed that the influence of resilience on the various dimensions of apathy diminishes as cognitive function declines. Specifically, utilizing the Johnson-Neyman 9 ARTICLE IN PRESS technique, we identified that when cognitive function scores fell below 26.03, the association between resilience and loneliness became statistically insignificant. This observation aligns with the study by Windle et al. (2021), which demonstrated that mental health resilience could predict loneliness over time when the MMSE score was below 25; however, this predictive power disappeared when the score was below 23, after controlling for covariates. Despite the scarcity of research exploring the interaction between resilience and loneliness across different levels of cognitive function, the precise mechanisms underlying this relationship remain unclear. Notably, the moderating role of cognitive function may reflect the essential role of cognitive flexibility in enabling resilience, a capacity often compromised in vascular-related cognitive decline. Vascular burden, particularly affecting front striatal circuits, has been linked to both apathy and reduced executive function (Hollocks et al., 2015; Zamboni et al., 2008). While our sample excluded individuals with overt vascular or coSgnitive diagnoses, subclinical pathology may still influence the resilience–apathy pathway. Such an approach P would further elucidate the complex biological context in which psychological resilience operates during the aging process. NevertheleNss, our findings provide further support for the I critical roles of resilience and cognitive function in helping middle-aged and older adults navigate challenging circumstances. This underscores the necessity for culturally sensitive and ecologically valid apathy assessments, which reflect the social values and structures of the target population. This pattern may further reflect culturally embedded gender roles, with older women deriving motivation more from family obligations and men from social peer networks, particularly post- retirement. These differences align with prior findings that Chinese women are often expected to maintain family cohesion, while men may derive self-worth from social engagement and status (Huang & Yang, 2013; Yi et al., 2024). Such sociocultural dynamics likely shape differential reporting of motivational behaviors on apathy measures. 10 ARTICLE IN PRESS 5. Limitations Some limitations should be acknowledged when interpreting the results of the present study. Firstly, although it is possible to observe moderated mediation effects when cognitive functions are relatively preserved, the incidence of apathy tends to be higher in populations suffering from dementia or other neurodegenerative diseases, where cognitive functions often fall within the deficit range. Secondly, our study utilized self-reported measurements to document the variable, which potentially presents challenges in avoiding self-response bias and response sets. Ultimately, it is essential to acknowledge that the potential for an inverse causal relationship cannot be ruled out due to the inherent limitations of our research design, which restrict our ability to establish causality among variables. Although our moderated mediation model conceptualizes resilience as a precursor that indirectly influences apathy through loneliness, the reverse pathway is theoretically plausible. For instance, individuals experiencing sustained apathy may gradually disengage socSially, leading to heightened loneliness and diminished resilience over time. Our crosSs-sectional design limits causal inference; therefore, future longitudinal studies are necEessary to examine these reciprocal R mechanisms further. Nonetheless, our model reflects one theoretically grounded perspective P consistent with existing frameworks on aging, adaptation, and motivation. Concisely, it is suggested that future studies employ a longituNdinal approach and combine alternative methods I of evaluation, such as informant-rated assessments, to validate further the impact of the moderated mediation model within theE population mentioned earlier. Conclusion C Employing a moderated mediation model, our study is a pioneering foray into the nexus I between resilience and muTlti-dimensional apathy in community-dwelling middle-aged and R older adults. The analysis revealed a significant indirect association between resilience and A multi-dimensional apathy, specifically through loneliness, within the domains of Cognitive and Social Motivation, and Spontaneous Behavioral Activation. Our findings highlight loneliness as a key intervention target in mitigating apathy among older adults. Social engagement programs and behavioral activation may be effective, especially when cognitive training is less feasible due to impairment. Resilience-building strategies such as mindfulness or cognitive-behavioral techniques may further buffer against loneliness and apathy. Future research should explore tailored, multimodal interventions based on individuals’ cognitive profiles and apathy subtypes. JSON: Name: resilience_loneliness_apathy_modmed Title: Moderated mediation analysis of resilience reducing multi-dimensional apathy via loneliness with cognitive function as a moderator in middle-aged and older adults Short Hypothesis: Higher psychological resilience reduces multi-dimensional apathy indirectly by lowering loneliness, and this indirect effect is attenuated as cognitive function decreases. Related Work: Prior work has established associations among resilience, loneliness, cognitive function, and apathy, and several studies have tested simple mediation or correlation-based models linking psychosocial resources to motivational outcomes. Existing approaches frequently rely on cross-sectional samples, single global apathy scales, and bivariate analyses that do not model conditional indirect pathways. Limitations in the literature include small samples underpowered to detect interaction effects, heavy reliance on self-report measures without parallel objective cognitive or neurobiological data, sparse examination of apathy subdomains, inconsistent control for depressive symptoms, and a lack of formal moderated mediation modeling. Neurobehavioral studies point to distinct neural substrates across apathy subtypes, but psychosocial moderators of indirect pathways remain understudied. Consequently, unresolved issues include whether loneliness mechanistically mediates resilience→apathy relationships across apathy dimensions and whether cognitive status systematically modulates that mediation across representative aging cohorts. Abstract: This research operationalizes and tests a moderated mediation model in which psychological resilience predicts lower multi-dimensional apathy via reduced loneliness, and where cognitive function moderates the resilience→loneliness path. The study addresses limitations of prior work by using validated multi-domain apathy instruments, an explicit moderated mediation framework, and comparisons across apathy subcomponents. The primary contribution is a pre-registered experimental pipeline specifying sample, measures, and statistical tests to determine whether the indirect effect of resilience on apathy through loneliness varies by cognitive function. Expected outcomes are: (1) a significant negative indirect effect of resilience on cognitive/social motivation and spontaneous behavioral activation apathy via loneliness, (2) an index of moderated mediation indicating attenuation of that indirect effect at lower cognitive scores, and (3) demonstration of measurement robustness across apathy instruments. Results will clarify mechanistic pathways linking psychosocial resources, social experience, and motivational deficits in aging and will guide targeted interventions conditioned on cognitive status. Experiments: Design: cross-sectional primary study with planned secondary longitudinal follow-up at 12 months. Sample: recruit N=500 community-dwelling adults aged 50+, stratified to include ≥120 participants with MMSE 24-26 and ≥60 with MMSE 27-30; exclusion criteria: diagnosed major neurocognitive disorder, active psychosis, recent stroke. Measures: resilience scale for older adults (RSOA), Elderly Loneliness Scale, Geriatric Apathy Scale (GAS) subscales (CSM, ERE, SBA) and AES for comparison, GDS-15, full neuropsychological battery (attention, executive function, memory) and MMSE, optional MRI for white-matter hyperintensity (WMH) quantification in a subsample (n≈150). Baselines: (A) simple linear regression resilience→apathy; (B) mediation model resilience→loneliness→apathy; (C) moderated mediation with cognitive function moderating resilience→loneliness (PROCESS Model 7); (D) alternative moderator models replacing cognitive function with depressive symptoms or social support. Statistical analysis: bootstrap (5,000 resamples) for indirect effect CIs, compute index of moderated mediation, report standardized coefficients, R-squared change, and model fit indices (for SEM: CFI, RMSEA, SRMR). Ablation/comparisons: (1) compare GAS vs AES for global apathy detection and subdomain sensitivity; (2) ablate loneliness to quantify direct versus indirect pathways; (3) ablate cognitive moderator to measure change in indirect effect magnitude; (4) include WMH as covariate in subsample to evaluate neurobiological confounding. Covariates: age, sex, SES, living arrangement, and GDS-15. Power: target 80% power to detect small-to-moderate interaction (f2≈0.02) given planned sample. Missing data: multiple imputation for <20% missingness. Pre-registration: hypothesis, analytic scripts, and planned contrasts pre-registered. Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-sectional design limits causal inference and directionality of mediation. Self-report scales introduce response and cultural bias; measurement invariance across subgroups may be violated. MMSE has ceiling effects and limited sensitivity for domain-specific cognition, reducing moderator precision. Interaction effects require larger sample sizes; planned N may still be underpowered for small moderated mediation effects in subgroups. Recruitment bias toward healthier, more educated, or more socially engaged participants may limit generalizability. Residual confounding by depressive symptoms or unmeasured medical comorbidities may inflate or obscure pathways. MRI subsample selection bias and limited MRI sample size reduce power to detect neurobiological confounders. Multiple comparisons across apathy subdomains increase false positive risk if not corrected. Model misspecification (e.g., omitted nonlinearities) can bias estimates. Longitudinal attrition and missing data patterns may bias follow-up analyses. Computational burden for SEM bootstrapping and multiple imputations may require substantial compute resources.
